Observability Foundations
Telemetry • Linux Monitoring • Metrics • Logs • Traces • SLIs/SLOs • Dashboards •

Chapters 1-10 | 2026 Edition
Production objective: build an observability foundation that can explain user impact, correlate
system behavior across signals, detect data-quality failure, and support safe operational
decisions - not merely display infrastructure graphs. Beginner to Production-Ready DevOps and SRE Engineering

About This Part
Volume 11 begins the observability, monitoring, logging, tracing, and Site Reliability Engineering sequence. Part
A establishes the concepts and operating contracts required before deep specialization in Prometheus, Grafana,
log platforms, OpenTelemetry, tracing backends, profiling, alert engineering, incident response, and enterprise
observability architecture. The core principle is that observability starts with user journeys, operational questions, ownership, and
trustworthy evidence. Tools are selected only after the required decisions, signals, context, reliability, security,
privacy, retention, and cost boundaries are understood. Foundation principle: a green dashboard is not proof of a healthy service, and missing telemetry
must never be silently interpreted as success. Volume 11 Roadmap

Scope, Safety and Cost Controls

Run load, failure, outage, network, storage, alert-routing, and data-loss tests only in disposable or explicitly
approved nonproduction environments.

Use synthetic services, identities, data, logs, traces, and secrets.

Run load, failure, outage, network, storage, alert-routing, and data-loss tests only in disposable or explicitly
approved nonproduction environments.

Use synthetic services, identities, data, logs, traces, and secrets. Never place production credentials,
customer data, internal hostnames, or employer configurations in course artifacts.

Apply storage quotas, retention, ingestion limits, sampling, budgets, and cleanup before generating high-
volume telemetry. Observability systems can consume substantial compute, memory, disk, network, and
managed-service spend.

Protect audit, security, trace, and log records according to their data classification. Telemetry can contain
personal data, tokens, paths, queries, payload fragments, and infrastructure identifiers.

Verify current product versions, supported configuration, image names, ports, licensing, feature status, and
official guidance before production deployment.

How to Use This Book
1. Read the operational question and architecture notes before running commands.
2. Build each lab in a disposable environment and capture timestamps, configuration, output, screenshots, and
cleanup evidence.
3. Generate known-good telemetry before introducing a controlled failure.
4. Validate normal, missing-data, delayed-data, duplicate-data, overload, failure, and recovery paths.
5. Explain each result in your own words and convert the lab into a sanitized portfolio artifact. Part A Learning Outcomes

Design an observability operating model with named users, questions, owners, service levels, trust
boundaries, retention, and cost controls.

Correlate metrics, logs, traces, events, profiles, resource context, release context, and platform self-
telemetry.

Troubleshoot Linux host and process behavior using CPU, memory, storage, network, service, and kernel
evidence.

Design metric and log schemas that aggregate correctly, avoid unbounded cardinality, and protect
sensitive information.

Define user-centric SLIs, SLOs, error budgets, dashboards, alerts, and runbooks.

Build and validate a small observability platform project with controlled failure and recovery exercises.

VOLUME 11A | CHAPTER 1
Chapter 1: Observability, Monitoring and the SRE Operating
Model
Understanding what must be known before choosing tools
Why this chapter matters: Teams often install dashboards before defining the decisions, users,
ownership, and failure scenarios the observability system must support. This creates telemetry
without operational clarity. Learning Objectives

Distinguish monitoring, observability, telemetry, diagnostics, audit evidence, and business analytics.

Explain how observability supports development, operations, security, reliability, and product decisions.

Define ownership, consumers, service levels, retention, and failure boundaries for an observability platform.

Use hypothesis-driven investigation instead of dashboard guessing.

Create a measurable foundation roadmap for a small service. Core Concepts
Monitoring and observability
Monitoring evaluates known conditions and objectives through selected measurements. Observability is the
capability to infer internal system behavior from externally available outputs, especially when the exact failure
mode was not predicted. Mature operations use both: monitoring for explicit decisions and observability for
explanation. Telemetry and evidence
Telemetry includes metrics, logs, traces, profiles, events, and contextual metadata. Evidence is telemetry that
has sufficient identity, time, integrity, retention, and interpretation to support a decision, incident timeline,
audit, or change review. Consumers and questions
Developers need code-level failure context; operators need service health and recovery signals; security teams
need identity and threat evidence; product teams need user-impact and business-flow measurements.

d questions
Developers need code-level failure context; operators need service health and recovery signals; security teams
need identity and threat evidence; product teams need user-impact and business-flow measurements. One
dataset may serve several consumers, but each question requires an explicit contract. SRE operating model
Site Reliability Engineering applies software engineering to operations. Reliability work is guided by service
objectives, risk, error budgets, automation, incident learning, capacity, and reduction of repetitive toil rather
than by an unlimited promise of uptime. Architecture and Operating Decisions

Start with user journeys and operational decisions, not with dashboard products.

Assign owners for instrumentation, collection, storage, visualization, alerting, retention, privacy, and
incident use.

Separate service telemetry from audit and security records when access, immutability, or retention
requirements differ.

Define what happens when the monitoring system itself is degraded or unavailable.

Review usefulness through incident outcomes, alert quality, investigation time, adoption, and cost.

operations: sre-oncall
user_journeys:
- submit-order
- retrieve-order-status
decisions:
- is the service meeting its latency and success objectives?
- is a new release harming customers?
- which dependency is responsible for an error increase?
required_signals: [metrics, structured-logs, traces]
monitoring_rto_minutes: 30
telemetry_retention_days: 30
review_interval: quarterly

☐ The platform has service objectives and a documented degraded-mode procedure.
☐ Investigation, alert, audit, privacy, and cost requirements are explicitly separated.
☐ A review process removes unused dashboards, noisy alerts, unowned data, and high-cost cardinality.

Hands-on Lab 1: Create an Observability Operating Charter
Prerequisites

A sample service or imagined production system.

A repository for diagrams, decisions, runbooks, and evidence.

At least three operational scenarios: release regression, dependency failure, and capacity saturation. Implementation
1. Identify the top three user journeys and the business consequence of failure.
2. List service components, dependencies, owners, environments, trust boundaries, and existing telemetry.
3. Write ten questions that engineers must answer during normal operation and incidents.
4.

onsequence of failure.
2. List service components, dependencies, owners, environments, trust boundaries, and existing telemetry.
3. Write ten questions that engineers must answer during normal operation and incidents.
4. Map each question to metrics, logs, traces, profiles, synthetic checks, or business events.
5. Define platform ownership, service objectives, retention, access, privacy, cost, and degraded-mode behavior.
6. Run a tabletop exercise in which the primary dashboard system is unavailable during an application incident.

7. Publish the charter, open gaps as tracked work, and schedule the first usefulness review. Validation Evidence

A service map and consumer-question matrix are version controlled.

Every critical question has an owner and at least one proposed evidence source.

The degraded-mode exercise produces a recovery or alternative-observation procedure. Cleanup

Remove any real production identifiers or customer data from the learning repository.

Close temporary accounts, tokens, dashboards, and test data created for the exercise. Interview Questions and Model Answers
1. What is the practical difference between monitoring and observability?
Monitoring evaluates defined conditions and objectives; observability helps explain internal behavior from
system outputs, including failures that were not fully anticipated.
2. Why is telemetry not automatically evidence?
Without reliable time, identity, context, integrity, retention, and interpretation, telemetry may be incomplete
or misleading for a decision.
3. Who owns observability?
The platform team may own shared capabilities, but service teams must own instrumentation and the
meaning of service-specific signals. Ownership must be explicit across the full pipeline.
4. How do you measure an observability platform?
Use signal availability, freshness, query performance, alert quality, investigation time, incident outcomes,
adoption, coverage, and cost rather than counting dashboards. Chapter Summary

Observability begins with questions, ownership, and user impact.

Monitoring and observability are complementary capabilities.

Telemetry requires context and validation before it becomes evidence.

The observability platform is itself a production service with failure modes and service objectives.

VOLUME 11A | CHAPTER 2
Chapter 2: Telemetry Signals and End-to-End Data Flow
Designing metrics, logs, traces, profiles, events, and context as one system
Why this chapter matters: Individual signals are useful, but incidents are resolved faster when
engineers can move from a user symptom to a service metric, correlated trace, structured log,
and resource context without losing identity or time. Learning Objectives

Explain the strengths and limitations of metrics, logs, traces, profiles, and events.

Design producer, receiver, processor, exporter, storage, query, and visualization stages.

Use consistent resource and service attributes to correlate signals.

Recognize data-loss, duplication, delay, ordering, sampling, and schema risks.

Design a vendor-neutral collection tier using OpenTelemetry concepts. Core Concepts
Metrics
Metrics are numerical measurements aggregated over time. They are efficient for trends, objectives, capacity,
and alerting but usually omit individual-event detail. Counters, gauges, histograms, and summaries have
different semantics and aggregation behavior. Logs and events
Logs record events with timestamps, severity, body, resource context, and attributes. Structured logs improve
parsing and correlation. Audit events require stronger integrity and access controls than ordinary diagnostic
logs. Traces and profiles
A trace represents a request or workflow as spans connected across services. Profiles attribute resource
consumption to code paths over time. Traces explain request flow; profiles explain where CPU, memory, or
other resources are consumed. Pipeline and context
A telemetry pipeline receives, enriches, filters, batches, samples, buffers, routes, and exports data.

races explain request flow; profiles explain where CPU, memory, or
other resources are consumed. Pipeline and context
A telemetry pipeline receives, enriches, filters, batches, samples, buffers, routes, and exports data. Resource
attributes, service identity, environment, region, version, trace identifiers, and synchronized time make cross-
signal analysis possible. Architecture and Operating Decisions

Use a stable service naming and resource-attribute convention across every signal.

Collect close to the source when local buffering, enrichment, or network isolation is required.

Centralize processing only when the capacity and failure-domain trade-off is acceptable.

Treat sampling and filtering as governed data-loss decisions with observable rates.

Define behavior for backpressure, exporter failure, queue exhaustion, and partial backend outage.

Hands-on Lab 2: Build and Validate a Local Telemetry Pipeline
Prerequisites

Docker or a local OpenTelemetry Collector binary.

A sample application or telemetry generator.

A repository for collector configuration and test evidence. Implementation
1. Create a Collector configuration with OTLP receivers, memory limiter, resource enrichment, batching, and
debug exporters.
2. Start the Collector and inspect its own startup and health telemetry.
3. Send one trace, one metric, and one log record from a sample application or telemetry generator.
4. Verify service name, environment, version, timestamps, trace ID, and span ID.
5. Stop the exporter destination or use an invalid endpoint to observe retry, queue, and failure behavior.
6. Restore the destination and determine whether queued data is delivered, dropped, or duplicated.
7. Document the data flow, ports, trust boundaries, failure modes, and production improvements. Validation Evidence

Collector configuration is version controlled and syntactically validated.

Known telemetry records appear with correct resource context.

Failure and recovery behavior is captured with collector self-telemetry. Cleanup

Stop and remove containers, volumes, generated data, and temporary certificates.

Delete test attributes that contain local usernames, hostnames, or sensitive paths. Interview Questions and Model Answers
1. When should you use metrics instead of logs?
Use metrics for efficient trends, objectives, aggregation, capacity, and alert conditions; use logs when event
detail and contextual fields are needed.
2. What is context propagation?
It carries identifiers and metadata across process and service boundaries so spans, logs, and related
operations can be correlated.
3.

detail and contextual fields are needed.
2. What is context propagation?
It carries identifiers and metadata across process and service boundaries so spans, logs, and related
operations can be correlated.
3. Why monitor the telemetry pipeline itself?
A silent collection failure can make a healthy-looking dashboard false. Pipeline freshness, drops, queues,
retries, errors, and capacity are part of system correctness.
4. What is the risk of centralizing all telemetry processing?
A central tier simplifies governance but can become a bottleneck, broad failure domain, sensitive-data
concentration point, and high-cost dependency. Chapter Summary

Signals answer different questions and should be correlated through stable context.

The collection pipeline can lose, delay, duplicate, or transform data.

Sampling and filtering are explicit risk and cost decisions.

Collector health and data quality must be observable.

VOLUME 11A | CHAPTER 3
Chapter 3: Service Inventory, Ownership and Observability
Requirements
Turning architecture and user journeys into measurable contracts
Why this chapter matters: Observability coverage becomes unreliable when teams do not know
which services exist, who owns them, which dependencies are critical, and what each
environment is expected to expose. Learning Objectives

Build a service catalog that links ownership, repositories, runtimes, dependencies, objectives, and
telemetry.

Classify services by criticality, data sensitivity, change rate, and support model.

Define minimum observability requirements as a versioned platform contract.

Identify blind spots, orphaned services, and unsupported telemetry paths.

Use onboarding and decommissioning workflows to keep inventory current. Core Concepts
Service inventory
A service inventory is an authoritative record of deployable and operational units, their owners, repositories,
runtime locations, dependencies, user journeys, data classifications, and lifecycle states. Criticality and tiers
Tiering should reflect business impact, recovery needs, dependency centrality, regulatory obligations, and
support model. Higher tiers require stronger objectives, synthetic checks, retention, alert coverage, recovery,
and review. Minimum telemetry contract
A contract defines required service identity, request measurements, dependency measurements, structured
logs, trace propagation, release annotations, dashboards, alerts, runbooks, and data-quality checks. Lifecycle governance
New services should satisfy onboarding gates before production. Retired services must remove alerts,
dashboards, credentials, collectors, storage, and ownership records to avoid stale cost and confusion.

cycle governance
New services should satisfy onboarding gates before production. Retired services must remove alerts,
dashboards, credentials, collectors, storage, and ownership records to avoid stale cost and confusion. Architecture and Operating Decisions

Choose an authoritative catalog and automate updates from source, deployment, and runtime evidence.

Require owners and escalation paths before a service enters a supported production tier.

Use platform defaults but allow documented exceptions with owner, risk, expiry, and review.

Track telemetry coverage and data quality as release-readiness signals.

Make decommissioning a first-class workflow rather than simply stopping workloads.

Hands-on Lab 3: Create a Service Catalog and Telemetry Contract
Prerequisites

Three sample services with at least one dependency relationship.

A Git repository or simple catalog file.

An agreed set of service tiers. Implementation
1. Define a service-record schema containing ownership, tier, repositories, environments, dependencies, data
classification, objectives, dashboards, alerts, and runbooks.
2. Create records for three services and intentionally leave one ownership field incomplete.
3. Write validation that rejects missing required fields for production-tier services.
4. Map runtime evidence to inventory and identify orphaned or unexpected workloads.

5. Define a minimum observability contract for each tier.
6. Create an exception record with owner, reason, compensating control, expiry, and review date.
7. Run a mock decommissioning and verify removal of telemetry and access artifacts. Validation Evidence

Schema and service records are version controlled.

Validation demonstrates both accepted and rejected records.

A drift or orphan report and decommission checklist are produced. Cleanup

Remove test integrations and catalog entries.

Delete temporary alert routes, dashboards, API keys, and generated service data. Interview Questions and Model Answers
1. Why is a service catalog relevant to observability?
Telemetry without ownership and service context cannot reliably route alerts, define objectives, control
retention, or support incident response.
2. How should service tiers be chosen?
Use business impact, user dependency, recovery requirements, data sensitivity, regulatory obligations, and
support model rather than team preference alone.
3. What belongs in an observability contract?
Identity, required signals, schemas, objectives, release annotations, dashboards, alerts, runbooks, retention,
access, quality checks, and exception handling.
4. How do you prevent a catalog from becoming stale?
Automate reconciliation from repositories, deployment systems, runtime inventory, and ownership
directories, then alert on drift and missing owners. Chapter Summary

Inventory and ownership are prerequisites for reliable telemetry.

Criticality should drive observability requirements.

Platform contracts standardize minimum behavior without hiding service-specific meaning.

Onboarding and decommissioning must update the full observability lifecycle.

VOLUME 11A | CHAPTER 4
Chapter 4: Linux Host and Process Monitoring Fundamentals
Reading CPU, memory, disk, network, process, and service behavior safely
Why this chapter matters: Application incidents often become confusing because engineers
cannot distinguish CPU pressure from load average, memory use from memory pressure,
filesystem capacity from I/O latency, or a listening socket from a reachable service. Learning Objectives

Inspect Linux load, CPU, memory, storage, network, processes, services, and logs.

Interpret rates and trends instead of relying on one snapshot.

Correlate application symptoms with operating-system evidence.

Use /proc and standard utilities without causing additional load.

Build a repeatable host investigation record. Core Concepts
CPU and scheduler
CPU utilization shows time categories; load average represents runnable or uninterruptible work relative to
available capacity. High load can result from CPU saturation or blocked I/O, so run queue, per-CPU activity,
process state, and latency must be interpreted together. Memory and pressure
Linux uses available memory for cache. Free memory alone is not a failure signal. Evaluate available memory,
swap activity, reclaim, major faults, cgroup limits, out-of-memory events, and application working set. Storage and network
Filesystem fullness is different from device latency and saturation. Network reachability is different from a local
listening socket. Inspect capacity, inodes, device queues, error counters, retransmissions, routes, DNS, firewall,
and application responses. Process and service context
Processes run under users, cgroups, namespaces, limits, and service managers. A healthy process identifier
does not prove the service is responsive, reachable, or meeting objectives.

esponses. Process and service context
Processes run under users, cgroups, namespaces, limits, and service managers. A healthy process identifier
does not prove the service is responsive, reachable, or meeting objectives. Architecture and Operating Decisions

Collect a lightweight baseline before an incident.

Use rate-based tools over an interval and record timestamps.

Begin with user symptom, then inspect service, dependencies, host pressure, and recent change.

Avoid destructive commands and high-frequency diagnostics on production without approval.

Link host telemetry to service, environment, instance, and deployment version.

uptime
free -h
vmstat 1 5
pidstat -dur 1 5
iostat -xz 1 5
ss -s
ss -lntup
ip -s link
df -hT
df -ih
systemctl --failed
journalctl -p warning..alert --since "15 minutes ago" --no-pager
# Process context
ps -eo pid,ppid,user,stat,%cpu,%mem,etimes,cmd --sort=-%cpu | head
cat /proc/pressure/cpu
cat /proc/pressure/memory
cat /proc/pressure/io

☐ User-path and dependency tests accompany host-level evidence.
☐ Commands, access, and outputs are sanitized before external sharing.

1. What does Linux load average measure?
It reflects the average number of tasks runnable or in uninterruptible sleep over time; it must be interpreted
relative to CPU capacity and I/O evidence.
2. Why can free memory be low on a healthy server?
Linux uses memory for page cache and reclaims it when needed. Available memory, swap activity, faults,
PSI, and OOM events are more useful than free memory alone.
3. How do you distinguish disk capacity from disk performance?
Capacity uses filesystem bytes and inodes; performance uses device throughput, queue depth, utilization,
latency, errors, and application I/O behavior.
4. Does a listening port prove a service is healthy?
No. It proves a local socket exists. Reachability, protocol behavior, dependencies, latency, correctness, and
user outcomes require separate validation. Chapter Summary

Linux diagnosis requires correlated rates, states, and timestamps.

Load, utilization, pressure, capacity, and latency are different concepts.

A running process or listening port does not prove service health.

Safe baselines make incident evidence faster and more reliable.

Chapter 5: Metrics and Time-Series Data Fundamentals
Designing measurements that aggregate correctly and remain affordable
Why this chapter matters: Poor metric semantics and uncontrolled labels can create misleading
dashboards, unusable alerts, and expensive time-series growth even when the monitoring
software is operating correctly. Learning Objectives

Explain time series, samples, labels, dimensions, scrape intervals, and aggregation.

Choose counters, gauges, histograms, and summaries correctly.

Apply naming, units, reset handling, and label-cardinality controls.

Recognize missing data, stale series, delayed samples, and aggregation errors.

Create service metrics for traffic, errors, latency, and saturation. Core Concepts
Time-series model
A time series is identified by a metric name and a set of dimensions or labels, with timestamped samples. Every
unique label combination creates another series, so dimensions are both analytical power and resource cost. Metric types
Counters increase except for reset and are analyzed as rates or increases. Gauges move up and down. Histograms count observations in configured buckets and support aggregation and quantiles. Summaries
calculate client-side quantiles that are generally difficult to aggregate across instances. Cardinality and identity
Unbounded values such as user ID, request ID, timestamp, email, or raw URL path should not become metric
labels. Keep high-detail identity in logs or traces and use bounded dimensions in metrics. Golden signals and RED/USE
Common service measurements include traffic, errors, latency, and saturation. RED emphasizes request rate,
errors, and duration for services. USE emphasizes utilization, saturation, and errors for resources.

and RED/USE
Common service measurements include traffic, errors, latency, and saturation. RED emphasizes request rate,
errors, and duration for services. USE emphasizes utilization, saturation, and errors for resources. These
frameworks guide discovery but do not replace user-specific SLIs. Architecture and Operating Decisions

Define metric meaning, type, unit, labels, owner, and expected cardinality before release.

Use base units and consistent naming conventions.

Prefer histograms for aggregatable latency distributions and choose buckets from real objectives and
traffic.

Record deployment version and stable service context, but avoid per-request labels.

Set cardinality budgets and monitor active series, churn, ingestion, and query cost. Reference Configuration or Command Pattern

1. Why should counters usually be queried as rates?
The raw value is cumulative and resets on restart. Rate or increase functions express change over time and
can account for resets.

2. What is metric cardinality?
It is the number of unique time series created by label combinations. High or unbounded cardinality

3. When would you choose a histogram?

Chapter 6: Logs and Structured Event Engineering
Creating diagnostic records that are searchable, correlated, secure, and governable
Why this chapter matters: Logs become expensive noise when they lack stable fields, severity
discipline, correlation identifiers, ownership, retention, and protection against secrets or
personal data. Learning Objectives

Distinguish diagnostic logs, audit logs, security events, and business events.

Create structured records with stable schemas and contextual fields.

Use severity, message design, trace correlation, and error classification consistently.

Design collection, parsing, buffering, indexing, retention, and access controls.

Prevent secret leakage, injection, duplication, and unbounded event volume. Core Concepts
Log classes
Diagnostic logs explain system behavior; audit logs record security-relevant actions; security events support
detection; business events describe domain outcomes. Their integrity, access, retention, and immutability
requirements can differ. Structured records
A useful structured log contains event name, timestamp, severity, service/resource identity, environment,
version, trace and span identifiers, outcome, error type, and bounded attributes. Human-readable messages
remain helpful, but fields support reliable queries. Severity and actionability
Severity should describe operational significance, not developer emotion. Repeated expected events should not
be emitted as errors. Alerts should not be created simply from every ERROR record without user-impact logic. Pipeline and governance
Agents or collectors read sources, parse and enrich records, buffer data, route by class, and export to storage.

rts should not be created simply from every ERROR record without user-impact logic. Pipeline and governance
Agents or collectors read sources, parse and enrich records, buffer data, route by class, and export to storage. Controls include schema validation, redaction, quotas, retention, immutability, access review, and legal or
privacy requirements. Architecture and Operating Decisions

Define event names and schemas as versioned interfaces.

Keep secrets, credentials, payment data, and unnecessary personal data out of logs by design.

Use trace and span identifiers to correlate records, but do not use them as metric labels.

Route audit and security records to appropriate protected storage.

Set volume budgets, sampling rules, retention, archive, and deletion by log class.

Chapter 7: Distributed Tracing and Context Propagation
Fundamentals
Following a request across services, queues, databases, and asynchronous work
Why this chapter matters: In distributed systems, a user-visible delay or failure may cross many
services and asynchronous boundaries. Without trace context and meaningful spans, teams
correlate timestamps manually and often blame the wrong component. Learning Objectives

Explain traces, spans, parent-child relationships, links, attributes, events, status, and resources.

Propagate context across HTTP, messaging, and asynchronous work.

Choose span boundaries and attributes that answer dependency and latency questions.

Understand head, tail, and probabilistic sampling trade-offs.

Correlate traces with metrics, logs, and releases. Core Concepts
Trace model
A trace represents an end-to-end operation. Spans represent timed operations with parent relationships,
attributes, events, status, and resource context. A trace is useful only when span names and attributes describe
actual service and dependency behavior. Propagation
Trace context is carried across process boundaries using protocol headers or message metadata. Missing or
overwritten context fragments a request into unrelated traces. Links can connect asynchronous or batch
relationships that are not strict parent-child operations. Instrumentation
Automatic instrumentation provides broad coverage quickly. Manual instrumentation adds domain operations,
important attributes, and meaningful events. Duplicate instrumentation, excessive spans, sensitive attributes,
and unstable names must be controlled. Sampling
Head sampling decides early and is simple but may discard rare failures.

ttributes, and meaningful events. Duplicate instrumentation, excessive spans, sensitive attributes,
and unstable names must be controlled. Sampling
Head sampling decides early and is simple but may discard rare failures. Tail sampling evaluates more
complete traces but requires collector state, latency, and capacity. Sampling policy must be observable and
aligned with incident and cost needs. Architecture and Operating Decisions

Use stable span names based on operations or route templates, not raw identifiers.

Propagate context through every supported protocol and asynchronous boundary.

Record errors and dependency attributes without placing sensitive payloads into spans.

Preserve representative baseline traffic while prioritizing rare errors or slow traces within budget.

Link traces to service metrics, logs, deployment version, and incident timelines.

Chapter 8: SLIs, SLOs, Error Budgets and User-Centric
Measurement
Defining reliability through what users experience
Why this chapter matters: Infrastructure health can remain green while customers experience
failures. Service objectives translate user expectations into measurable indicators, decision
rules, and balanced reliability investment. Learning Objectives

Distinguish SLIs, SLOs, SLAs, error budgets, and operational targets.

Select availability, latency, quality, freshness, durability, and correctness indicators.

Define valid events, good events, windows, exclusions, and data sources.

Calculate budget consumption and burn rate conceptually.

Connect objectives to alerting, release, incident, and prioritization decisions. Core Concepts
SLI, SLO and SLA
An SLI is a measured property of service behavior. An SLO is the target level over a defined window. An SLA is a
business agreement that may include consequences. Internal objectives should support decisions even when no
external agreement exists. User-centric indicators
Useful indicators approximate what users care about: successful requests, latency below a threshold, correct
results, fresh data, durable writes, or completed business workflows. Easy infrastructure measurements are
supporting evidence, not substitutes. Windows and budgets
An objective such as 99.9% good events over 30 days permits 0.1% bad events. The error budget is the allowed
unreliability. Burn rate describes how quickly the budget is being consumed relative to the allowed rate. Decision policy
Objectives should state what happens when budget is healthy, at risk, or exhausted. Responses may include
investigation, release caution, reliability work, or executive risk acceptance.

the allowed rate. Decision policy
Objectives should state what happens when budget is healthy, at risk, or exhausted. Responses may include
investigation, release caution, reliability work, or executive risk acceptance. Error budgets should guide
judgment, not become an automatic punishment mechanism. Architecture and Operating Decisions

Start from user journeys and consequences, then work backward to measurable indicators.

Define numerator, denominator, thresholds, window, exclusions, source, owner, and data-quality checks.

Use multiple windows or burn-rate views to detect fast and slow objective risk.

Separate service objectives from monitoring-system availability and internal component targets.

Review objectives when user expectations, architecture, traffic, or business risk changes.

VOLUME 11A | CHAPTER 9
Chapter 9: Dashboards, Alerting and Diagnostic Workflow
Foundations
Building views and notifications that drive correct action
Why this chapter matters: A dashboard is not useful because it contains many panels, and an
alert is not useful because it detects every anomaly. Both should support a specific decision
with trustworthy context and a clear next action. Learning Objectives

Design dashboards for service overview, investigation, capacity, release, and platform health.

Apply hierarchy, units, thresholds, time ranges, variables, and annotations correctly.

Distinguish records, notifications, tickets, and pages.

Write actionable alerts with severity, ownership, runbook, and inhibition or grouping behavior.

Use a systematic investigation workflow based on symptoms, scope, change, dependencies, and evidence. Core Concepts
Dashboard purpose
Overview dashboards answer whether users are affected and where to investigate. Diagnostic views support
deeper component analysis. Capacity and release views answer different questions and should not be mixed
into one wall of panels. Visualization integrity
Correct units, axes, aggregation, denominators, rate windows, missing-data treatment, and time alignment
matter more than visual decoration. Annotations for deployment and configuration changes reduce
investigation time. Alert actionability
A page should require timely human action for material impact or objective risk. Tickets and notifications can

1. What makes an alert actionable?
It represents material impact or risk that requires a timely human decision and includes ownership, context,
evidence, and a safe next action.
2. What should appear first on a service dashboard?
User journey and objective status, then traffic, errors, latency, saturation, dependencies, changes, and
telemetry health.
3. Why add deployment annotations?
They help correlate a symptom with changes without assuming every incident was caused by the latest
release.
4. How do you reduce alert fatigue?

missing data, route accurately, and review alert outcomes. Chapter Summary

Chapter 10: Foundation Observability Platform Project
Integrating service inventory, Linux telemetry, metrics, logs, traces, SLOs, dashboards, and alerts
Why this chapter matters: The foundation is complete only when a second engineer can deploy
the stack, generate a known incident, observe user impact, correlate evidence, execute
recovery, and verify that telemetry remains trustworthy. Learning Objectives

Design a small but production-informed observability architecture.

Deploy Prometheus, Grafana, node-level metrics, a sample service, and an OpenTelemetry collection path.

Create structured logs, traces, service metrics, an SLO, dashboard, alert, and runbook.




Minimum viable platform
The project includes a sample service, host metrics, service metrics, structured logs, traces, collection, storage,
visualization, objective calculation, alerting, ownership, runbooks, and platform self-monitoring. Trustworthy validation
A successful container start is not validation. Test the user path, known telemetry, timestamps, labels,
correlation, objective calculation, alert routing, recovery, and data-loss behavior. Failure exercises
Introduce bounded failures: stopped service, dependency latency, CPU pressure, collector outage, scrape
failure, and invalid configuration. Each exercise needs a hypothesis, stop condition, evidence, recovery, and
post-test cleanup.

unded failures: stopped service, dependency latency, CPU pressure, collector outage, scrape
failure, and invalid configuration. Each exercise needs a hypothesis, stop condition, evidence, recovery, and
post-test cleanup. Portfolio evidence
A credible project contains architecture, repository structure, configuration, ADRs, service records, SLO,
dashboard source, alert tests, runbook, incident timeline, measured results, known limitations, cost estimate,
and next steps. Architecture and Operating Decisions

Use Docker Compose or an isolated lab cluster with explicit resource limits and cleanup.

Keep the architecture simple enough to understand every data path.

Pin images or versions for reproducibility and record resolved digests where possible.

Use synthetic data and never embed real credentials or production configuration.

Treat the platform as a service with health checks, storage, retention, backup, and recovery tasks.

Hands-on Lab 10: Build the Volume 11A Observability Foundation
Prerequisites

Docker Engine with Compose, or an approved isolated lab cluster.

At least 8 GB RAM and sufficient temporary disk space.


A Git repository and synthetic sample service.

No production credentials, identifiers, or customer data. Implementation
1. Create the repository structure for app, Prometheus, Grafana provisioning, OpenTelemetry Collector, service
catalog, SLO, alerts, runbooks, tests, and evidence.
2. Deploy the sample service, Prometheus, Grafana, node exporter, and Collector with pinned versions and
bounded resources.
3. Instrument service metrics, JSON logs, and a two-span trace; apply consistent service, environment, and
version context.
4. Create a service record, one user-centric SLO, a service overview dashboard, and an actionable alert with
runbook.
5. Generate normal, failed, slow, and saturated traffic and validate metrics, logs, traces, SLI, dashboard, and
alert lifecycle.
6. Stop one collection component and one service component separately; observe data freshness, platform
health, user impact, recovery, and possible data loss.
7. Publish architecture, ADRs, test results, incident timeline, cost/retention assumptions, limitations, cleanup,
and the backlog for Volume 11B. Validation Evidence

A fresh environment can be deployed from version-controlled configuration.

A reviewer can follow one request through service metric, structured log, and trace.

The SLO and alert respond correctly to controlled failure and recovery.

The final report includes platform self-monitoring and data-loss findings. Cleanup

Export sanitized evidence, then run docker compose down -v or the equivalent approved teardown.

Remove images, volumes, generated data, local credentials, temporary DNS, and firewall changes not

1. What proves an observability platform works?
Known telemetry and user-path tests must traverse collection, storage, query, visualization, alerting, and
recovery with expected identity, freshness, and data quality.
2. Why test telemetry failure separately from service failure?
A service outage and an observation outage create different risks. Without separate testing, missing data
may be mistaken for healthy behavior.
3. What should be included in a portfolio observability project?
Architecture, code, service catalog, instrumentation, objectives, dashboards, alerts, runbooks, failure drills,
evidence, trade-offs, cost, security, and limitations.
4. What is the next technical depth after this foundation?
Prometheus architecture, exporters, service discovery, PromQL, recording rules, Alertmanager, scaling, high
availability, federation, and long-term metrics operations. Chapter Summary

The capstone integrates all Volume 11A foundations.

End-to-end validation matters more than successful startup.

The observability system must expose its own health and data quality.

The completed project becomes the base for advanced Prometheus engineering in Volume 11B.
